You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

{"title":"How to Make Your Dog Visible at Night: Safety Tips for Dark Evening Walks","meta_description":"Learn how to make your dog visible at night with a clip-on LED light, reflective gear, a well-fitted harness and a simple night-walk checklist.","slug":"how-to-make-your-dog-visible-at-night","markdown":"The best way to make your dog visible at night is to layer two things: an active light that glows on its own, and reflective gear that bounces back car headlights. Add a well-fitted harness, a short leash and a bit of visibility for yourself, and dark evening walks become a lot safer and a lot less stressful. Here's how to put it all together.

## Why dogs disappear in the dark

Dogs are surprisingly hard to spot after sunset. Many have dark or brindle coats that blend straight into the shadows, and even light-coloured dogs can look like just another patch of grey under streetlights. They're also low to the ground, which puts them below the main sweep of a driver's attention and often in the dimmer part of a headlight beam.

The result is that drivers, cyclists and runners tend to see a dog late, sometimes only when it's already close. On a quiet path that might mean a startled jogger; near a road it can be much more serious.

It helps to understand the two ways you can make your dog easier to see:

- **Being lit (active visibility):** a light that produces its own glow. It works whether or not anyone is shining a light at your dog, so people can see it from any direction.
- **Being reflective (passive visibility):** materials that only shine when light hits them, such as car headlights or a torch beam. They're excellent for drivers, but they do nothing in total darkness.

The safest setup uses both, so each one covers the gaps of the other.

## Light them up: using a clip-on LED light

An active light is the single most effective step you can take, because it makes your dog visible to everyone around you, not just to people with headlights pointed your way.

Our [Rechargeable LED Collar Light](P1) clips onto any collar or harness, so it works with the gear your dog already wears [F1]. It's visible from about 1,000 ft [F3]. That kind of early warning gives drivers and cyclists time to notice your dog, slow down and give you space.

### Where to attach it

Aim for a spot that stays visible from as many angles as possible. The top of the collar or the back of a harness usually works well, since those areas aren't hidden by your dog's legs or chest as they move. Because the light clips onto either a collar or a harness, you can move it to whichever position suits your dog's shape and coat [F1].

### Steady or flashing?

The light has three modes: steady, slow flash and fast flash [F2]. Each one has its place:

- **Steady:** a constant glow makes it easier for people to judge exactly where your dog is and which way it's moving. Good for parks, paths and quieter streets.
- **Slow flash:** a gentle pulse that stands out against other lights without being too intense.
- **Fast flash:** the most attention-grabbing option, useful near busier roads or in places with lots of competing light, like shop fronts and traffic.

### Battery life, charging and wet weather

The light runs for 6 hours on steady mode, which comfortably covers an evening walk or several [F5]. It's rechargeable and charges via USB-C, so you can top it up with the same cable you use for many everyday devices [F4, F8]. It's also rated IPX7 waterproof, so rain, puddles and a dog who can't resist a stream don't have to cut the walk short [F6].

{{P1}}

## Add reflective gear for headlight visibility

Reflective materials are built to bounce light back towards where it came from. When car headlights hit a reflective strip, a good chunk of that light returns straight to the driver's eyes, so your dog suddenly lights up in their view. That's why reflective gear is so effective near roads.

The catch is that reflective gear needs a light source pointed at it. A driver coming towards you will see it, but someone approaching from a dark side path won't. That's why it works best as a backup layer alongside an active light rather than as your only line of defence.

Reflective details on the gear your dog wears every day are an easy win, because they're always there even if you forget to grab anything else. Our [Front-Clip No-Pull Harness](P2) is a harness with reflective stitching [F9, F15]. Paired with a clip-on light, you get a glow people can see from any direction plus extra shine whenever headlights sweep across your dog.

## Keep control when visibility is low

Visibility is only half of night-walk safety. A dog that suddenly lunges after a fox, a cat or a dropped takeaway carton is a much bigger risk in the dark, when drivers have less time to react and you have less time to spot what set your dog off.

### How a front-clip harness helps

A front-clip harness gives you more steering power than a collar or back-clip harness. On our Front-Clip No-Pull Harness, the leash ring sits on the chest and turns your dog sideways when it pulls [F12]. That sideways turn makes it harder for your dog to build up forward momentum, which is exactly what you want on a dark pavement next to traffic.

It also has a padded neoprene chest plate, so the front of the harness sits comfortably on your dog's chest [F14]. If you're weighing up different styles, our guide on [how to choose a dog harness](L3) walks through the options.

### Get the fit right

A harness that slips or twists can let a determined dog back out of it, and that's the last thing you want at night. Our Front-Clip No-Pull Harness has four adjustment points, so you can fine-tune it around your dog's neck and chest for a snug, secure fit [F13]. It comes in sizes XS, S, M, L and XL [F11]. Across those sizes it fits a chest girth of 13–42 in [F16]. Measure your dog before choosing, and check our [harness size guide](L6) if you're between sizes.

As a quick check, you should be able to slide a couple of fingers under the straps, but the harness shouldn't rotate or slide back over your dog's shoulders when you give the leash a gentle tug.

{{P2}}

### Keep the leash short near traffic

Long lines are brilliant for recall training in open spaces, but near roads in the dark they give your dog far too much room to wander into the path of a car or bike. Stick to a standard-length leash for night walks on streets and pavements, and save the long line for daytime sessions in safe, open areas. Our [leash length guide](L4) explains which length suits which situation.

## Make yourself visible too

Your dog is only one half of the team. If a driver sees a glowing dog but not the person attached to it, they may still misjudge the space you both need.

- **Carry a light:** a headlamp keeps your hands free for the leash and poo bags, while a handheld torch is handy for scanning the path ahead and spotting hazards before your dog does.
- **Wear bright or reflective clothing:** a reflective vest, jacket or armband makes a big difference to how early drivers notice you. Light colours help under streetlights, but reflective details do the heavy lifting in headlight beams.
- **Walk facing traffic where there's no pavement:** this lets you see oncoming cars and step aside in good time, and keep your dog on the side away from the road.
- **Stay alert:** keep headphones quiet or off so you can hear approaching cars, bikes and other dogs.

## A quick night-walk checklist

Before you head out on a dark evening, run through this quick list:

1. **Charge the light.** Top up the LED collar light via USB-C so it's ready to go [F4].
2. **Clip it on.** Attach the light to your dog's collar or harness where it's easy to see from several angles [F1].
3. **Check the harness.** Make sure the fit is snug and secure, and that the reflective stitching on the harness isn't covered by a coat or caked in mud [F15].
4. **Use a short leash.** Leave the long line at home for street walks.
5. **Choose well-lit routes.** Stick to lit streets and familiar paths where you can, especially in bad weather.
6. **Carry a torch or wear a headlamp.** Make sure you're as visible as your dog, and wear something reflective too.

With a light on your dog, reflective backup, a secure harness and a bit of visibility for yourself, dark evenings can be just as enjoyable as daytime strolls. You'll find everything for your night-walk kit in our [walking gear collection](L1)."}
